title: Why Do Pigeons Bob Their Heads 5 Times a Second? 🐦
description:
Why do pigeons bob their heads when they walk? The head thrusts forward, then holds still in space while the body catches up, which keeps the bird's view of the world steady, and a 1978 treadmill experiment showed the bobbing stops when the surroundings don't move.

topic: Why do pigeons bob their heads when they walk?
script: Pigeon heads never bob, you've been watching them freeze in midair. Watch one walk, the head shoots forward, about two inches. That's the thrust. Then it stops dead, locked in place, while the body walks underneath it. That's the hold. Then forward again, five to eight times every second. But why bother? In nineteen seventy-eight, scientists in Canada put a pigeon on a treadmill. Its legs kept walking, but the world around it stayed still, and the bobbing stopped. So it isn't about balance, it's about what the bird sees. Holding its head still keeps the view steady, like a camera on a tripod, while the world slides past. Chickens and cranes do it too. So next time you see a pigeon, watch the head. Is it bobbing, or standing still?
key_facts: The head thrusts forward about 2 inches relative to the body, then holds still in space while the body moves forward (Michael Land via Live Science; Journal of Comparative Physiology A 2007 via Snopes).
This happens on average five to eight times a second while walking (Aaron Blaisdell via Live Science).

In 1978, researchers at Queen's University in Canada found the bobbing stopped when a pigeon walked on a treadmill with stationary surroundings, pointing to a visual response rather than balance (Live Science, Snopes).
